title: Activities fail a WCAG 2.1 AA Success Criterion when zoomed at 400%
body:
Reported on forums by OU [link]
Xerte activities fail WCAG 2.1 AA Success Criterion ([…] when zoomed at 400%. The header and footer obscures the body content. Please view attachment. Please advise if this can be corrected.

I don't think the header is the problem but the footer is because it's position is absolute rather than moving with the content. I think this overlaps with another desirable change that some ask for where the footer is sticky but moves with the content if needed rather than being absolute. e.g. https://philipwalton.github.io/solved-by-flexbox/demos/sticky-footer/

So two issues I think:
Solving this issue with the current structure
Changing the structure (perhaps via an optional property) so it's possible to have a sticky footer rather than absolute footer.

I guess one of the problems might be that I think there are page types that currently calculate sizes and positions that might be affected by a change like this?

CSS tricks have what is perhaps a relevant article on different ways to implement a stick footer https://css-tricks.com/couple-takes-sticky-footer/

title: Logical focus- and reading order between markers and popups
body:
_Raising this issue on behalf of @timveld._

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The focus order ("tab order") between markers (or other elements bound to popups) and popups is not logical.

This is due to markers and popups existing in different subtrees of the DOM (`leaflet-marker-pane` and `leaflet-popup-pane`).

A [logical focus order is [link]) so that (all) users can:

> encounter information in an order that is consistent with the meaning of the content and can be operated from the keyboard. This reduces confusion by letting users form a consistent mental model of the content.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

@timveld's https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet/issues/7968#issuecomment-1069147811:

> - Ensure that the popup appears immediately below the marker in the DOM

**Additional context**

- Current behavior fails WCAG [[…] Focus [link])
- [web.dev: DOM order matters](https://web.dev/dom-order-matters/)

title: Ensure users can control the visual presentation of text
body:
The user should have comprehensive controls over the presentation of text within a webpage.

Ensure that:

-     Foreground and background colors can be selected by the user
-     The width of text is no more than 80 characters or glyphs (40 if [CJK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJK_characters))
-     Text is not justified (aligned to both the left and the right margins)
-     Line spacing is at least a space-and-a-half within paragraphs, and paragraph spacing is at least 1.5 times larger than the line spacing
-     Text can be increased to up to 200% size without assistive technology, without requiring the user scrolls horizontally to read a line of text on a full-screen window

For further details, see [Understanding Success Criterion [link]).

title: Check images have been correctly defined as decorative
body: Images with empty alternative text (e.g. `alt=""`) are considered decorative, and are ignored by assistive technology. You should check that these images are safe to ignore. Decorative images and are defined by W3C as "serving only an aesthetic purpose, providing no information, and having no functionality". Note that if an image serves a purpose which is identical to adjacent text, it can be correctly marked as decorative. For example, the `alt` here is redundant: ```css Apple ``` Accessible technologies will tend to see this as "Apple Apple". The correct behavior is to specify either a null (empty) `alt` attribute: ```css Apple ``` This check purposely ignores images which define an explicit [presentation role](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Roles/presentation_role), for example: ```css ``` In comparison to empty alt attributes, the use of a role is almost always intentional. For further details on this check, see [Understanding Success Criterion [link]).

title: Consider preventing page scroll when modal dialog is visible
body:
Another UX/a11y improvement for the `dialog` element would be to ensure that, when in the modal state, the underlying document cannot be scrolled.   This will help ensure that the invoking element for the dialog will remain in the visible viewport, and when focus is returned to the document, the viewport will not have to re-scroll to ensure this element is in view.  This topic was originally surfaced by Curtis Wilcox on the web a11y slack channel.

I have created a quick demo to show how the underlying document is presently scrollable while the modal dialog is visible: https://codepen.io/scottohara/full/YzYGpNy

One caveat I can think of with this idea is that if an author makes a dialog that is too large for the current viewport, then the underlying document will _need_ to be able to scroll so as to allow someone to view all the content of the dialog.

Though, one could also argue that this could be, at least partially, mitigated by setting a max-height/width to the dialog so that it does not extend beyond the bounds of the browser viewport.  Authors will need to do something like this to some degree to meet [[…]: [link]).

title: Accessible font icons
body: We use icon fonts in many places. In this post I propose the consistent use of three patterns of embedding the font icons to ensure their accessibility. There are basically two types of icon fonts: * **stand-alone icons** that convey meaning, semantic icons * **decorative icons** illustrating the accompanying words. ### Decorative icon Decorative icons express the same meaning as the accompanying words. We use them to visually enhance the meaning of the illustrated words. If we remove them from the page, users will still fully understand the content and will be able to use the page. Such icons do not have to be announced to users of screen readers. We should hide them from screen readers. To hide the icon font from screen readers, we use the `aria-hidden="true"` attribute. Add it to the tag with the icon font. For example: ```html ``` ### Stand-alone icon Stand-alone (semantic) icons convey meaning by themselves. They cannot be removed from the page without losing meaning or functionality. Since some users may not see the graphic symbols, we should pass their content in an alternative text. This is an elementary accessibility requirement specified in WCAG 2.1 by […]. Stand-alone icons can be interactive elements, e.g. buttons, switches, links and "normal", non-interactive content elements. #### Non-interactive icons If the icon is not an interactive element: * hide the icon from the screen readers using the `aria-hidden="true"` attribute, * provide a label for sighted users of the mouse using `title` attribute, * provide alternative text visible only to screen readers using `sr-only` class. For example: ```html Meaning of the icon ``` #### Interactive icons If the icon is an interactive element: * provide the accessible icon name to the screen readers using the `aria-label="ActionName"` attribute. * hide the icon from the screen readers using the `aria-hidden="true"` attribute. * provide a label for sighted users of the mouse using `title` attribute, **Note** that in this case you do not have to create a hidden element with alternative text only for screen readers. For example: ```html ``` ```html ` ``` Note that the `title` attribute with label is added to the tag with the icon hidden from the screen readers, as opposed to the `aria-label` attribute. As a result, screen readers do not repeat the label twice. ### Digression In the discussion on PR [Make ActionButton Featured accessible #23718](https://github.com/joomla/joomla-cms/pull/23718) I withdrew from the suggestion to add a `title` attribute to provide an accessible name for sighted users. The PR author's argument that the meaning of the icon would be understandable from the context (column name) seemed convincing. **After thinking about it, I have to say that it was a wrong decision.** The `title` attribute is necessary (**or any other way of providing alternative text for sighted users**). Otherwise, the meaning of the icon may be incomprehensible to some users. No alternative text violates the [[…] Non-text [link]): > All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for the situations listed below. > **Controls, Input**: If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, then it has a name that describes its purpose. **Note**: The problem can be solved using **tooltips**: https://codepen.io/dgrammatiko/pen/eGELjo ### See: * [Font Awesome & Accessibility. Make your icons awesome for all of

title: [EuiCallout][COGNITION]: Document consumer responsibility with `header` prop
body:
## Description
@cchaos and @1Copenut were discussing the  callout `heading` prop [defaulting to a P tag](https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/5870#discussion_r866349095) in PR #5870 5870. We opted to leave the default as a P tag for now and open an exploratory ticket for improved awareness. We want consuming applications to be aware callouts should have a relevant heading that is properly nested (H4 if under an H3 for example) when it makes sense.

Making sure callouts have proper headings is especially important if the text is styled in such a way as to suggest prominence or greater importance than paragraph text.

There are two items we'd like to look at specifically:

1. Callout guidance in the `EuiCallout` docs page outlining why a properly nested heading is important for assistive technology. I'll list some relevant links below.
2. Making the `heading` prop required by consuming apps in the future. This feels like a good defensive coding strategy. It also has potential to be a breaking change.

title: [EuiTable][SCREEN READER]: Expanding a row causes the "parent" row to be removed from cursor navigation flow
body:
## Description
Our `EuiTable` component has a feature to include [expanding rows](https://eui.elastic.co/#/tabular-content/tables#expanding-rows). While testing this as part of the data grid expandable rows discussion #5638, I confirmed an issue @constancecchen noted where clicking a button to expand a row causes it to be removed from the screen reader cursor navigation flow.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Assume MacOS - Start Safari and navigate to our [EuiTables - expanding rows](https://elastic.github.io/eui/#/tabular-content/tables#expanding-rows) section
2. Start VoiceOver
3. Expand a row by clicking on the `Expand` button at the end of a row
4. Navigate to the next row with `Ctrl + Opt + arrow key`
5. Try to navigate back to the previous row by pressing `Ctrl + Opt + UP_ARROW`
6. Confirm the row that triggered the new row is being skipped

## Possible solution example
I mocked up a new direction [based on Constance's feedback](https://github.com/elastic/eui/discussions/5638#discussioncomment-2200238) in the expandable rows discussion. My basic solution does not include React, just semantic HTML and basic CSS and JS to show how we could make expandable content into an accordion-like pattern in a single table cell: https://github.com/1Copenut/vanilla-accessibility-js/tree/main/table-expandable-content

## Guidance
- [aria-owns is not currently supported by VoiceOver on MacOS or iOS](https://a11ysupport.io/tech/aria/aria-owns_attribute)
- [Understanding […]: Info and [link])

title: [EuiButton] Disabled buttons are invisible to screen readers, creating a UX gap
body:
## Description Our use of the HTML `disabled` attribute on buttons removes them from the accessibility tree, making them invisible to screen readers and keyboard users and preventing us from providing critical context to all users. We should use `aria-disabled` instead. ## Problem to solve ### Pervasive accessibility issue in EUI (and Kibana by extension) Our buttons all use the HTML5 `disabled` attribute to remove buttons' default behavior. As a user, seeing a button as disabled (rather than not at all) often provides critical context for users. They see it, so they know there is an option to take some action, but that action not possible right now. For example, imagine a "Submit" button that is disabled. As a user, you'd see that button, now that you can take that "Submit" action, but it's not possible right now because there's something else you need to do first. To further help provide that context, we often provide tooltips on those buttons that provide additional context. "This button is disabled because you need to do XYZ first.". This is all useful context, all of which is invisible to screenreaders. They have no knowledge of the existence of that button or the additional context provided. ``` This button is disabled because you need to do XYZ first.

} > Submit ``` ### Common point of friction for development teams Teams often experience churn when they encounter this issue and find there's no current solution. Here's an example: https://github.com/elastic/kibana-team/issues/1323 ### Current workarounds One "workaround" (which is not really a feasible workaround) would be to not use `disabled` prop and apply all required handling manually as well as re-adding disabled styles. Another could potentially be to add focusable wrappers with e.g. tooltips instead. ### Examples in Kibana Recent requests or related issues or discussions: - https://github.com/elastic/eui/issues/8955 - https://github.com/elastic/eui/issues/8869 - https://github.com/elastic/eui/issues/4797
Slack threads - https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7QC1JV6F/p1749071324516399 - https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7QC1JV6F/p1749562984990239 - https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7QC1JV6F/p1728313799137969 - https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7QC1JV6F/p1726497255260529 - https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7CSV2REU/p1714131301706329
## Proposed solution To improve this behavior we want to replace the usage of the `disabled` attribute on button DOM elements with `aria-disabled`. This means: - the element is still announced in a disabled state to assistive technologies - the default behavior of `disabled` does not apply = the element has still all default events and behaviors Because the default disabled behavior is removed, we'll need to manually ensure the element behaves as if it was disabled. This means: - ensuring no unwanted events are triggered (e.g. unsetting of mouse and key events) - ensuring the disabled styling is applied based on the prop `disabled` not the DOM attribute via the selector `:disabled` - adjust all test cases that check disabled states ### Considerations 1. Based on the amount of different components that would benefit from this update (within EUI as well as on consumer side) we should consider providing a sharable solution (e.g. a hook) to provide the "set-_as_-disabled" functionality. 2. Updating a basic attribute like `disabled` might result in a lot of broken tests depending on testing framework and how those handle the check for "isDisabled". It would be wise to run tests/CI early with an early PoC to gage the impact and potential issues early on. - ⚠ Testing-library's `toBeDisabled` does not include `aria-disabled` ([issue](

title: Create prototype of form error summary pattern

## What

Create a working prototype pattern for a form error summary. The pattern should include the following:

- An error summary container at the top of the form, which confirms there has been an issue when submitting the form.

title: Accessibility: VoiceOver not announcing accordion aria-expanded state
Format devices, entities, and areas as tables for accessibility
body:
## Checklist

- [x] I have updated to the latest available Home Assistant version.
- [x] I have cleared the cache of my browser.
- [x] I have tried a different browser to see if it is related to my browser.

## The problem


The configuration pages showing the lists of devices, entities, and areas show the information visibly in tabular format, but they are not semantically marked up as tables in the HTML code.  This is required for assistive technologies such as screen readers to accurately present the content to the user and to allow the user to navigate efficiently.  Not marking them as tables is a failure of the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).  See [WCAG success criterion [link]).

## Expected behavior


Tables should be marked up semantically using `<table>`, `<tr>`, and `<td>` (or equivalent ARIA markup).  Relevant WCAG sufficient techniques are:
- [H51: Using table markup to present tabular [link])
- [H63: Using the scope attribute to associate header cells and data cells in data [link])
- [H43: Using id and headers attributes to associate data cells with header cells in data [link])

## Steps to reproduce


Try using a screen reader such as the free open source NVDA software to quickly work with and edit devices or entities.  It's painful.

## Environment



- Home Assistant release with the issue: Unknown
- Last working Home Assistant release (if known): Unknown
- Browser and browser version: This problem is browser independent
- Operating system: This problem is OS independent

title: Layers control should not expand on focus
body:
- [ ] I've looked at the [documentation](http://leafletjs.com/reference.html) to make sure the behavior is documented and expected
- [x] I'm sure this is a Leaflet code issue, not an issue with my own code nor with the framework I'm using (Cordova, Ionic, Angular, React…)
- [x] I've searched through the issues to make sure it's not yet reported

> **Note** <ins>Issue updated per https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet/pull/7057/files#r406663620.</ins>

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Visit https://leafletjs.com/examples/layers-control/example.html;
2. <kbd>Tab</kbd> until the layer control is focused;
3. Observe how <s>in Chrome</s> the layers list is expanded<s>, in Firefox it is not expanded</s>.

**Expected behavior**

The layers list should only be expanded after the layer control has been pressed.

I believe this is the original intent, as described in https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet/issues/6946#issuecomment-567620007 (emphasis mine): "the default collapsible `L.Control.Layers` can be navigated via keyboard: _**tab-focus on the collapsed layers control, then enter**_, then tab-focus on the set of radio boxes or on the checkboxes."

**Current behavior**

Layer list is expanded <s>in Chrome</s> <ins>(in all browsers)</ins> when the layer control recieves focus.

**Environment**
- Leaflet version: <s>[…]</s> <ins>[…]</ins>
- Browser (with version): Firefox 77.0.1 / Chrome 83.0.4103.116
- OS/Platform (with version): Windows 10

**Additional context**

Having the layers list only expand after the layer control has been pressed would also meet […], the "[Understanding […]: Bypass [link])" documentation lists several benefits of hiding content (such as a layer list) behind a menu, including:

> - People who use only the keyboard or a keyboard interface can reach content with fewer keystrokes. Otherwise, they might have to make dozens of keystrokes before reaching a link in the main content area. This can take a long time and may cause severe physical pain for some users.

title: Feature tabbing bypass blocks
body: > That's a convention sometimes referred to as "skip links": https://webaim.org/techniques/skipnav/. > Here's an example: https://genericcomponents.netlify.app/generic-skiplink/demo/index.html. > > It works by using a CSS hack to visually hide the links and unhide them as they recieve focus. There is no standard way to hide something that's intended to be focusable (related discussions, FWIW: https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/560, https://github.com/w3c/css-a11y/issues/13). > > It's indeed helpful, it relates to SC [[…] Bypass [link]). I suppose I can see a standard implementation of it (both as a CSS property and as a default facility in maps) but I think that's also based on assumptions of how users currently interact with maps (and what is keyboard accessible, under which circumstances). _Originally posted by @Malvoz in https://github.com/Maps4HTML/Web-Map-Custom-Element/issues/264#issuecomment-768606392_ Was discussing with Ahmad, we think having a forward/backward bypass block mechanism built into the (popup) UI would be helpful / essential. When you tab to a feature, then tab into its (popup) UI, the tab sequence could include a fast forward/backward affordance to get to the end of the feature tab sequence quickly. So the "normal" tab-through-features sequence would be interruptible by drilling into one feature and activating its bypass block. [image]

title: Feature request: Switch TableBlock’s header controls to a field that requires user input
body:
### Is your proposal related to a problem?

Related: #5865, #5977. Wagtail’s [TableBlock](https://docs.wagtail.io/en/v[…]/reference/contrib/table_block.html#tableblock) has support for defining the first row, or column, as table headers. 

While it’s not mandatory for a table to have header cells, if the table isn’t meant for layout then using header cells is a usability and accessibility benefit (or requirement) – header cells are generally displayed differently (e.g. bold), and screen readers will use the header cell’s label when announcing items is the header for. I believe failing to mark up header cells as such is a failure of [WCAG2.1’s […] (Info and [link]).

I think the current form makes it a bit too easy to miss those checkboxes and leave the table without headers.

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would suggest changing the header cells’ two checkboxes to a single "Header cells" dropdown, with the following options:

- [Choose] (Default)
- First row
- First column
- First row and first column
- No header cells

This field would be required. The main improvement here is the fact that contrary to checkboxes, the field has to be interacted with for the user to select the "No header cells" option that we want to discourage the use of (but should still be an option).

### Describe alternatives you've considered

One alternative would be to do this as a per-project customization, but it feels like an improvement that could easily live in Wagtail directly. Other changes to the TableBlock to remove the ability to have no header cells aren’t particularly compelling, because we still want the ability to select row/column/both.

### Additional context

Additionally to the above, as part of this change we could consider:

- Improving the help text for this field, to clarify its usage and the accessibility consequences
- Adding a straightforward way to customize this to disable the "No header cells" option – in practice all data tables should have header cells, and a table that doesn’t have any would be better as a list, or heading sections

In terms of migration, this looks like it could be easy:

- First row checkbox -> First row dropdown option
- First column checkbox -> First column dropdown option
- Both checkboxes -> "Both" dropdown option
- No checkboxes -> "No header cells" option

title: date-time-picker: requires horizontal scrolling at small viewport sizes
body:
## WCAG Level
Level AA

## Priority
Medium

## Pages/screens/components affected
* [Date Time Picker](https://vaadin.com/docs-beta/latest/ds/components/date-time-picker/)

## Description
Browsers have functionality that lets people zoom in on the page, enlarging all of the content in equal proportion. If zoom hasn't been taken into consideration when designing the page, it can result in 2 Dimensional scrolling (both horizontal and vertical) being needed to view the content.

The related WCAG 2.1 success criterion states that it should be possible to zoom into a website presented in "standard" desktop size (generally accepted to be 1280 x 1024 pixels) to 400% without 2D scrolling occurring.

At a viewport width of 320 CSS pixels, the date-time-picker leads to horizontal scrolling.

[image]

## User impact
When zooming causes horizontal and vertical scrolling it makes it hard to read the content because scrolling up/down and left/right disrupts the reading flow. If someone has mobility difficulties in addition to having low vision they may lack the dexterity needed to scroll in different directions, making the content completely inaccessible.

## Required solution
Make sure that content adapts/reflows to fit a 320 CSS px width viewport, so that scrolling in two directions is not necessary. Also make sure content is not cut off and unreachable at this viewport width.

This solution must be applied to all instances of the issue identified within the test sample, then applied to all other instances of the same issue identified throughout the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website.

## Implementation guidance
In this case, we would recommend allowing the two separate sub-components (the date picker and the time picker) to stack vertically depending on the available viewport width.

## Test procedure(s)
Use these steps to confirm that the solution has been correctly applied to issues identified within the test sample, and to test the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website for instances of the same issue:
1. Open the page in a browser.
2. Set the size of the browser to a "standard" desktop size (approximately 1280px wide).
3. Zoom content to at least 400%.
4. Check that the content reflows to a single column and that it can be viewed without both horizontal and vertical scrolling being necessary (with exceptions for certain specific elements like tables, graphs, maps)

### Definition of done
Complete all of these tasks before closing this issue or indicating it is ready for retest:
* All issues identified within the test sample have been resolved.
* The rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website have been tested for the same issue.
* All issues identified throughout the rest of the components/website have been resolved or filed as new issues.

## Related standards
* [[…] (Level [link])

## More information
* [W3C: Technique […]: Failure of […] due to content disappearing and not being available when content has [link])
* [Knowbility: Exploring […]]([link]

## Test data
Test date: March 2021
Website: [vaadin.com/components](https://vaadin.com/components/), [vaadin.com/docs-beta](https://vaadin.com/docs-beta/latest/ds/components/)

title: a11y: Remove filter control is not keyboard focusable/actionable
body:
## Description:
The remove filter (x) control is an anchor element that is missing an `href` attribute and value. This makes the link inert/placeholder in browsers and is not keyboard focusable or actionable. This is the same issue as #136, but in a slightly different form.

## Screenshot:
[image]

## WCAG SC:
[[…] (Level [link]): All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints.

## Recommended fix:
Use a `button` element, if possible or [`input type="image"`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input/image) with the appropriate `alt` text to indicate "remove this filter" (not "close").

Browsers have functionality that lets people zoom in on the page, enlarging all of the content in equal proportion. If zoom hasn't been taken into consideration when designing the page, it can result in 2 Dimensional scrolling (both horizontal and vertical) being needed to view the content.

The related WCAG 2.1 success criterion states that it should be possible to zoom into a website presented in "standard" desktop size (generally accepted to be 1280 x 1024 pixels) to 400% without 2D scrolling occurring, and without any loss of content or functionality.

By default, the combo box component's popup adapts correctly the the browser's viewport, even at relatively small sizes. In the example for [Popup Width](https://vaadin.com/docs-beta/latest/ds/components/combo-box/#popup-width), however, the popup is explicitly set to be at a particular size, which leads to its contents overflowing a horizontal viewport of 320 CSS pixels. As the documentation site also suppresses horizontal scrolling (or at least the presence of a horizontal scrollbar), the overflowing content is essentially cut off and unreachable for desktop users with high magnification.

[image]

## User impact
When zooming causes horizontal and vertical scrolling it makes it hard to read the content because scrolling up/down and left/right disrupts the reading flow. If someone has mobility difficulties in addition to having low vision they may lack the dexterity needed to scroll in different directions, making the content completely inaccessible.

In this case - at least for the documentation site - horizontal scrolling is not possible, meaning that users will be unable to read any of the overflowing content altogether.

## Required solution
Make sure that content adapts/reflows to fit a 320 CSS px width viewport, so that scrolling in two directions is not necessary. Also make sure content is not cut off and unreachable at this viewport width.

This solution must be applied to all instances of the issue identified within the test sample, then applied to all other instances of the same issue identified throughout the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website.

## Implementation guidance
In this particular case, despite the author having specified a popup width, consider effectively overriding their choice if the end result would mean a popup that is wider than the viewport width.

## Test procedure(s)
Use these steps to confirm that the solution has been correctly applied to issues identified within the test sample, and to test the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website for instances of the same issue:
1. Open the page in a browser.
2. Set the size of the browser to a "standard" desktop size (approximately 1280px wide).
3. Zoom content to at least 400%.
4. Check that the content reflows to a single column, that it can be viewed without both horizontal and vertical scrolling being necessary (with exceptions for certain specific elements like tables, graphs, maps), and that content/functionality is not cut off.

title: Communicate “page breaks” via more than just styles
body:
As a screen reader user, I want page breaks to be available in text, so that I can perceive them.

Currently, page breaks in the preview document are only perceivable through visual styles. They should also be available in the text a screen reader announces to users.

---

At a minimum, I think we should add some sort of aria element to indicate page breaks to screen readers.

The draft WCAG 2.2 spec adds [[…] Page Break [link]) and includes these docs on [understanding the [link]) and [techniques for meeting the criterion]([link]

I think the minimum I mentioned above is sufficient for compliance, although we may consider adding the recommended navigation to the document. My only hesitation is that the navigation would not necessarily match what’s in the generated PDF document—I think we would need to use more advanced techniques to determine the pages that will be in the generated PDF.

title: a11y: External/new window icons missing text equivalent
body:
## Description:
The external/new window icons on links are rendered using a CSS generated background image which does not have the ability to offer text alt with it like a foreground image would. This means that screen reader users who cannot see the icon do not get the same information as a sighted user does.

## Screenshots:
[image]
[image]

## WCAG SC
[[…] (Level [link]): All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose...

## Recommended fix:
Either of the following fixes would be appropriate for this issue:
- Use a foreground image of the icon (instead of CSS generated background image) with `alt` set to "opens in new window", or...
- Use visibly-hidden text within the link text (apply `.usa-sr-only` class to the `span`) to append "- opens in new window" to the link text, or...
- Remove `target="_blank"` and `.usa-link--external` class from the links.

title: progress-bar: animation cannot be stopped
body:
## WCAG Level
Level A

## Priority
Medium

## Pages/screens/components affected
* [Progress Bar](https://vaadin.com/docs-beta/latest/ds/components/progress-bar/)

## Description
The progress bar indeterminate mode has an animation that is continuous until the progress is complete. As this may be for any period of time and is not confined to user instigated actions, it could cause issues for susceptible users.

## User impact
Someone with a vestibular disorder may find that constantly animated content makes them feel nauseous. Other people who have issues that affect their ability to focus may be distracted by the animation.

## Required solution
It must be possible to pause or stop any animations that:

* starts automatically
* lasts more than five seconds
* is presented in parallel with other content

If possible implement a method of preventing animations from playing in advance. If this is not possible, ensure there is an accessible method of pausing the animation.

## Implementation guidance
The simplest solution is to check for the `prefers-reduced-motion` CSS media feature. This is a well supported feature that allows users to configure, usually at the operating system level, a preference for reduced motion.

It can be used as follows:

``` css
@media screen and (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  :host(:not([aria-valuenow])) [part="value"]::before,
  :host([indeterminate]) [part="value"]::before {
    animation: vaadin-progress-pulse3 1.6s infinite cubic-bezier(.645, .045, .355, 1);
  }
}
```

The result of this CSS is that the animation will only be applied if the user has not set a preference for reduced motion.

You can provide an alternative style that targets only those users who have set a preference for reduced motion:

``` css
@media screen and (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  …
}
```

## Test procedure(s)
Use these steps to confirm that the solution has been correctly applied to issues identified within the test sample, and to test the rest of the website for instances of the same issue:
1. Identify all animated content
2. Ensure that there is at least one method of either preventing the animation before it starts or pausing it after it starts.

title: a11y: Pagination links need more info/context for screen reader users
body:
## Description:
Other than the `nav` region labelled as "pager", the pagination links are only announced as the characters within the link text without much context about them. 

## Screencast (VoiceOver experience of the pagination):
https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1093423/105545150-fc34f900-5cb8-11eb-92a0-ae5bd3ddbcbd.mp4

## WCAG SC
[[…] (Level [link]): Information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text.

### Additional Resources:
- [A11y Style Guide - Pagination](https://a11y-style-guide.com/style-guide/section-navigation.html#kssref-navigation-pagination)
- [VISA Global Accessibility Requirements - Pagination](https://developer.visa.com/pages/accessibility/navigation/nav-007)

## Recommended fix:
1. Update `aria-label` for the pager `nav` elements to something like "Search results pagination" (OK for this to be present twice on the page).
2. Add `aria-label` to the pager links to override the link text with something like "page 2", "page 3", etc.
3. Add `aria-label` to the "<" and ">" links to read something like "Previous page" and "Next page", respectively.
4. Add attribute `aria-current="page"` to the current page in the list.
5. Consider making the tap/click target area larger for people using touch devices and those with motor disabilities/disabilities involving fine motor control.

Note: these edits will match closely with the A11y Style Guide pagination example.

title: a11y: Filter results - no indication that filter selection changes result set
body:
## Description:
When a filter is selected/applied, the results set is updated on the page. There is no indication for screen reader users that the content has changed after a filter selection is made, so people may not know their choice(s) took effect.

## WCAG SC
[[…] (Level [link]) For all user interface components (including but not limited to: form elements, links and components generated by scripts), the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; **and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.**

### Additional guidance:
- Example site: [WCAG 2 Quick Reference (with [link]): Note that there is an `aria-live` region for announcing the addition or removal of filters which uses the code `<span id="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">` around the text that changes when filter changes occur. This helps to inform screen reader users about their changes in real-time with equivalent information that sighted users receive.

## Recommended fix:
Consider wrapping the applied filters content before the results in an `aria-live` region so that changes to the content in that area will be announced in real-time as the user makes their selections in the filter area(s).

title: context-menu: small-screen nested menus and mouse hover
body:
## WCAG Level
Level AA

## Priority
High

## Pages/screens/components affected
* [Context Menu: Nested Menu Items](https://vaadin.com/components/context-menu/html-examples/context-menu-items-demos)

## Description
Content (such as a dropdown menu or a popover) that appears when a user hovers a pointer (such as a mouse) over, or moves focus to, a particular section of the page can often cause problems for users. The content must be dismissable without the need to move the mouse or keyboard focus. The newly displayed content must be hoverable (i.e. not disappear once the users moves their mouse/focus from the element that caused the content to appear). And lastly, the content should be persistent, and not disappear after a set timeout while the user is still focused on, or hovering over, the trigger element or the content itself.

In the case of small screens/viewports, the `context-menu` with nested menus is extremely difficult to use for mouse users. As soon as the mouse hovers over a context menu item with a submenu, the submenu is opened, covering the previous level in the hierarchy. It is possible for the user to return to the previous level in the menu structure by clicking on the semi-transparent overlay above the context menu, or by pressing the left cursor key (although this is likely not what a user would expect). However, if a mouse user triggers the hover behaviour, and then - without moving the mouse - presses the left cursor key, the submenu is closed but then immediately reopened. If the user tries to close the submenu using `Esc`, the entire context menu is closed.

[image]

## User impact
The current behaviour of nested context menus in small viewport/screen scenarios likely assumes that these will be operated by touchscreen (although thankfully they also still work correctly for keyboard users). Low vision users use screen magnification or increased zoom settings, while still operating web content with the mouse. For these users, the current "open on hover" behaviour of the context menu will be frustrating and confusing.

## Required solution
In this particular case, the simplest solution is to remove the "open on hover" behaviour of the submenus when the context menu is in small screen view. Instead, only open the submenu when the user explicitly clicks on/activates the item with the submenu.

This solution must be applied to all instances of the issue identified within the test sample, then applied to all other instances of the same issue identified throughout the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website.

## Test procedure(s)
Use these steps to confirm that the solution has been correctly applied to issues identified within the test sample, and to test the rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website for instances of the same issue:
1. on a small screen/viewport, open a nested context menu
2. hover over items with a submenu
3. verify that the items don't open the submenu on hover
4. click on the items
5. verify that submenus open on click

### Definition of done

* All issues identified within the test sample have been resolved.
* The rest of the components, their variants, and the documentation website have been tested for the same issue.
* All issues identified throughout the rest of the components/website have been resolved or filed as new issues.

title: Documentation - best practice: use of color / theme variants
body:
## Pages/screens/components affected
* [Button](https://vaadin.com/components/button/html-examples)

## Description
When information is presented using colour, for example to indicate that an element has been selected, that same information must be available without colour or people who have difficulty seeing colours may not be aware that an item was indeed selected.

The [Colors](https://vaadin.com/components/vaadin-button/html-examples/button-theme-variants-demos#colors) section of the button documentation shows various examples of themed buttons for "Error" and "Success". Authors may end up using these variants to convey additional meaning to controls, relying solely on colour.

[image]

## User impact
When colour is the only way information is presented, people with low vision or colour blindness may not be able to perceive this.

In this case, unless it's obvious from context, or from the actual button text itself, these users may not be able to distinguish buttons that also provide information about the type of action they perform, or their current state, only through colour.

## Required solution
We would recommend, as a best practice, to add a note in the documentation, reminding authors that they should not rely on colour alone to convey meaning/information.

title: Best practice - grid-pro: editable column headers don't convey their interactive nature
body:
## Pages/screens/components affected
* [Grid Pro](https://vaadin.com/docs-beta/latest/ds/components/grid-pro/)

## Description
Editable cells currently don't convey the fact that they are editable to assistive technology users.

[image]

## User impact
When an assistive technology user reaches an editable grid cell, their screen reader will not announce the cell any differently from a regular "static" cell. Unless it's clear from the context, users may not even be aware that a cell is editable.

## Suggested solution
There is no one clear programmatic solution to this particular issue. One approach that we would suggest is to make sure that the column header (if all cells in that column are editable, but cells in other columns aren't) could contain a hint, such as additional "(editable)" text, to inform users. Alternatively, this could be conveyed as part of an instruction/description. Lastly, if a table can include a mix of static and editable cells (not just limited to a column - any cell in a table could be either editable or static), another approach may be to include "editable" as part of the accessible name of those cells. This could be combined with the use of an actual visible icon (like a little edit/pen icon), acting as its text alternative. This would then benefit all users, not just assistive technology users.

It may be advisable to also mention this to authors in the documentation.

## Test procedure(s)
Use these steps to confirm that the solution has been correctly applied to issues identified within the test sample, and to test the rest of the website for instances of the same issue:
1. Turn on your screen reader
2. Navigate through the grid with editable cells.
3. Verify that editable cells announce the fact that they are, in fact, editable.

title: Web Accessibility Checklist
body:
[link to the post](https://websitesetup.org/web-accessibility-checklist/)

# 1) Too Much Content

In brief: break up text into sections with headings and bulleted lists. Use simple language.

It’s well-known that as the number of choices increases, so does the effort required to collect information and make good decisions. It’s the same with too much content—it soon becomes overwhelming. Paring down content to the essentials is a time-consuming craft; as Mark Twain (allegedly) wrote: “I didn’t have time to write a short letter, so I wrote a long one instead.”

The recent book Writing Is Designing suggests

  >  People want to be able to skim long blocks of text, regardless of sight or audio, so it’s extremely important to structure your longform writing with headers, short paragraphs, and other content design best practices.

So:

  -  Have only one <h1> on a page.
  -  Use sub-headings liberally; it breaks up a ‘slab’ of text for sighted users, while users of assistive technologies such as screen readers can use a short-cut key to jump between headings or obtain a mental map of the content from the heading structure.
  -  Don’t skip a level of headings. For example, if you use an <h3>, make sure it is preceded by an <h2>.
  -  Use bulleted lists (like this!) marked up correctly in HTML as <ul>, <li>. Screen readers will announce “List of 10 items” (and allow the user to jump over them).


# use plain english

We now have 25 years of empirical research leading to an inescapable conclusion: if you want to please and persuade your reader, write in plain English.

# 2) ReCAPTCHA

In brief: don’t make your users jump through potentially impossible hoops in order to save developer time.

Respondents were often talking about an old ReCAPTCHA version:

[image]
The wobbly letters style of reCAPTCHA is now deprecated. It’s much more common to see a newer incarnation called “No CAPTCHA reCAPTCHA” (also known as the “I’m not a robot” Checkbox) which requires the user to check a box confirming they’re not a robot and which uses secret voodoo to score the user. If they pass, no further interaction is required. However, if they fail, a further challenge will be displayed:

Bear in mind that the type of CAPTCHA that requires a user to click all squares with (say) a street sign isn’t necessarily international. As Terence Eden writes, CAPTCHAs don’t prove you’re human – they prove you’re American.

The most accessible form of reCAPTCHA is reCAPTCHA v3 which requires no user interaction, but needs you to do more work to deal with visits that fail the test:

It is a pure JavaScript API returning a score, giving you the ability to take action in the context of your site: for instance requiring additional factors of authentication, sending a post to moderation, or throttling bots that may be scraping content.


# 3) Poor Legibility


  -  Ensure adequate contrast. One of the most common access blockers on the web is poor contrast between text and background. The W3C guidelines require a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for large-scale text and images of large-scale text which should have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 (logos and ‘incidental’ text are exempt). There are many utilities that can measure contrast ratios for you; my personal favorite is Ada Rose Cannon’s excellent contrast widget, which is a useful browser bookmarklet that highlights areas of insufficient contrast on your page.
  -  Don’t have all-capital headings. There’s evidence that they are harder to read because capital letters are all the same height, so we can’t recognize the shape of common words. Additionally, some screen readers will spell out groups of capital letters as if they were abbreviations (like BBC, DOJ, etc). If you must have all capital headlines, write them in a normal case in your HTML and transform them with CSS text-transform: uppercase.
  -  Left-align text. (For pages in right-to-left languages like Ara

title: The language of text track's cues is not marked programmatically when they are displayed
body:
## Description
WCAG 2.0/2.1 [[…] Language of [link]) requires that "The human language of each passage or phrase in the content can be programmatically determined ...".

Text tracks (captions, subtitles, and descriptions) may be in any language, and in particular, they may be in a different language from the rest of the content of the page in which they are displayed. Therefore, the text track may not be in the language indicated by the `lang` attribute of the HTML page, or [the `lang` attribute of the player](https://github.com/videojs/video.js/blob/main/src/js/player.js#L804).

Text tracks have a `srclang` attribute which, if present, indicates the language of the text track; this language attribute should be applied as a `lang` attribute either on the whole region that displays the track's cues or on each cue that is displayed.

Specifically, at https://github.com/videojs/video.js/blob/main/src/js/tracks/text-track-display.js#L421, a CSS style is applied to each text track display element according to the track's language; this could also be used to set the `lang` attribute of that element.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Go to https://videojs.com/advanced?video=elephantsdreammp4

title: surface view-level `h1`s (or equivalents) in page `title`s ([…])
body:
Per #5972:

> * The page `<title>` must be accurate and informative.
> * If a page is the result of a user action or scripted change of context, the text of the `<title>` should describe the result or change of context to the user.
> * The `<title>` should be concise.
> * The page `<title>` should be unique, if possible.
> * Unique information should come first in the `<title>`.
> * The page `<title>` should match (or be very similar to) the top heading in the main content. 

A few belated notes per <https://github.com/freedomofpress/securedrop/pull/6725#pullrequestreview-1252731682>:

1. Since the SecureDrop logo is our default `h1` across views, the "equivalents" here will usually be the per-view `h2`.
2. If the SecureDrop Web apps were larger (had more views), or if titles were more complicated or personalized, it might be worth setting the page `title` automatically from these headings.  As it is, a simple fillable Jinja `{% block title %}Your Title Here{% endblock %}` is adequate, even though it requires developers to keep the title in sync manually.
3. ~[We do need sign-off from our security engineers and UX designer](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jZlKco2YgOrrI4PmTkG_Q8lKuV5VxCds/edit?disco=AAAAIplLpt8), to whom I'll flag this question in a comment below.~  (resolved per <https://github.com/freedomofpress/securedrop/issues/6313#issuecomment-1411389401>)

title: Link underlining is inconsistent, not robust for accessibility
body:
# Problem

Links inside of surrounding text (sentences) have underlines, which is AWESOME and helps satisfy [[…] Use of [link]).

However not all links inside surrounding text have underlines, and there are several styles:
- No underline - default style from `a { text-decoration: none; }`
- Solid underline - e.g. from `.messages a { text-decoration: underline;}`
- Dashed underline - from `p a, .content a { `
- Solid and Dashed underline (two lines) - happens when a link matches two selectors.

This creates confusion - doe the different link styles convey a different meaning?

# Where

- Menu UI help page - `admin/help/menu_ui`
  This has a mixture of dashed underlines and no underlines.
  [image]

- Getting started box - `admin/help`
  This has a mix of solid underline, and solid-dashed-double underline
  Solid underline comes from `.message a {text-decoration: underline }`.
  The solid-and-dashed double underline is due to matching `.messages a` and `p a` selectors.
  [image]

 # Recommendation

1. Use a single underline for links inside surrounding text.  Make this the DEFAULT style, i.e. `a { text-decoration: underline; }`.   This is super-highly recommended for accessibility, and is the most reliable way to avoid [WCAG F73: Failure of […] due to creating links that are not visually evident without color [link]).  It's also a long-standing convention, and it's how the web looks before designers break it ;-)  See also:
    - [On Link Underlines](http://adrianroselli.com/2016/06/on-link-underlines.html)
    - [WebAxe: Keep the Underline](http://www.webaxe.org/keep-the-underline-text-links/)

2. Get rid of lots of other selectors, such as `.messages a` and `pa, .content a`.  You won't need them once you've done the previous steps. 

3. For links that are not inside surrounding text, AND have some other visual affordance (e.g. they are items in a toolbar), it's safe to override with a more specific selector like `.toolbar a`.

4. [aside] - if you want to use an alternative fancy link style, like underlining in a different colour, the new CSS4 [`text-decoration-*`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-decoration-color) are the preferred way, but there's no MSIE support.  Note that `border` is much more robust than `box-shadow`.  This is because some assistive tech which provides alternative colour spaces will selectively override/ignore some CSS.  For example, Windows High Contrast mode respects border style + width, and overrides border-color (so the border is still seen).  However Windows High Contrast causes  `box-shadow` to be stripped out entirely, so it won't be seen.

title: Allow icons to have title text for acccessibility
body: When icons are the only element inside a link, the link will not contain any text and will fail […]. The purpose of a [`<title>` element inside the `<svg>` element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Element/title) is to provide a short description of the graphic and will not be displayed by the browser other than, possibly, as a tooltip.

title: a11y: 3 tab stops for every book, all leading to same place (plus bad link text)
body:
https://next.smashingmagazine.com/printed-books/

Steps:

Tab to and past the first book on the page.

Expected:

As all links for the books (image, title, and read more) all go to the same place, I'd expect only one tab stop

Actual:

3 for every link, making it more frustrating to navigate the page. Futher more the image and read more link have weak link text, making it harder to navigate with screen reader too (no alt text, and "learn more -> respectively)

This fails WCAG due to:

"When adjacent links go to the same location (such as a linked product image and an adjacent linked product name that go to the same product page) this results in additional navigation and repetition for keyboard and screen reader users."

The lack of alt text and context to read more is additionally part of […]

Additionally the tab order is kind of strange as it tabs first to the image down the right side of the block, then back up again to the title, then the read more.

How I often solve these issues is by pinning and stretching the link/button to the full size of the element, such as:

* remove anchor from around the image, and set alt=""
* remove the anchor from inside the H3
* set position relative on the containing element
* set position: absolute, top, left, right, and bottom; 0 for the a::before (using whatever class it uses)

This way the before will fill the entire containing element and be clickable with only one tab stop. In this case the area is fairly big so not sure if you'd want it all to be clickable. 

If you do this you need to make the learn more anchor have acceptable accessible name. You can for example use aria-label="learn more about [[title of book]]" or use aria-labelledby to point to the ID of the h3.

Alternatively I'd put the alt="" on the image again and wrap the anchor around both the image and the h3. This will give one tab stop and the correct accessible name. That won't solve the learn more button being a duplicate though.

title: [Accessibility Bug] DDG needs tab default, visible focus outlining ([…])
body:
Copied from a previous Reddit post -- it took me far too long to find DDG's actual GitHub and actually fin a place to actually report bugs.

Please move if this is not the right repo, but this is explicitly related to CSS. I have hacked together a solution that only kind of works, and ultimately does not solve the problem.

My browser hack:
[image]

___

I use a keyboard to navigate my computer. I've noticed that DDG:

- doesn't have visual focus indicators (on anything, really)
- only inconsistently lets me tab to search results (if I watch the URL preview on the bottom of the browser)
- menus have odd behavior (don't open/close on keyboard focus or losing focus)

It's really hard to tell if there's any spots to report feedback like this, other than Reddit, unfortunately. Are there any devs I could work with or otherwise available spaces to discuss and work on these issues with?

Even Chrome can't display it's browser default, which tells me that visual focus is explicitly disallowed somewhere.

I love using DDG but, sorry, Google has ya beat here. These are simple issues, [and is required by [link]) More specifically, this [violates (fails) [link]).

**Privacy and accessibility do not, should not, and cannot be mutually exclusive - we already get the short end of the stick online. Even worse, there is no proper method to convey problems like this, or any accessibility contact information to be found on the site.**

I have since found out that there are keyboard shortcuts provided by DDG, but:

The shortcuts help (a lot, stylistically, visually), but that's not the default navigation expectation for keyboard users (hence my ignorance of the feature). As users decide to come to DDG from other search providers or browsers, they are not oriented to that, and won't go to search out a custom solution - they will expect the web-standard defaults to work. For me, it is MUCH more uncomfortable, and an unnecessary hurdle, to first tap M then use up and down arrows, when the tab key is a one stop shop for the entirety of the web - and requires no custom maintenance or JS!!

Keyboard shortcut styling:
[image]

(This looks and makes so much more sense. It could be more contrasty, but is a step in the right direction.)

**Especially since I was drawn from Firefox's omnibox**, I never once learned that DDG has keyboard shortcuts or themes beyond the standards - I have no reason to seek out the DDG homepage or help documents. I simply thought this was something DDG didn't care about.

**The focus indication provided by the custom solution could be/should be the default** - that'd be even better than most big search giants who just do underlining.

Google's tab focus (uses browser default rather than something better):
[image]

And they have skip links!!
[image]

I never knew (or forgot) about the expanded theme options, either. However, they all also lack visual focus using default behavior, even the "contrast" theme, which is the one I'd have suspected included it.

title: Minor accessibility issues with general layout
body:
* [ ] The page ID tab looks highlighted and shows it has a connection to the main content but that is not programmatically determinable.
It could at least have some hidden text, like "Page ID: ", to explain what it is and what the connection is to the page.
That fails [[…] Info and [link]).
[image]


## Other non-fail accessibility issues

These don't strictly fail WCAG but are still accessibility issues. Fixing them is recommended but optional for passing WCAG.

* [x] The header, footer, navigation and main content should be marked up as such (with `header`, `footer`, `nav` and `main`) to help screen reader users navigate the page.
This was fixed in #3432.

* [ ] Repeated blocks (tools, TOC, sidebar) have hidden headings but they are not in hierarchy. This could confuse screen reader users a bit, especially when those headings come after the main heading.
#3306 would fix that. See also #3299.

* [ ] There are usually two `h1`s on the page, the wiki title with logo and the first heading in the main content. The preview view has even three `h1`s (the third being "Preview"). It is best practice to give the one heading the lowest level which describes the page, so usually the first heading in the main content. A lot of screen reader users navigate by heading, some would skip straight to the first `h1` in order to skip to the main content. That wouldn't work in this case. But the main thing is to stay consistent.

title: Page tools less usable for low vision users
body:
* [ ] When resizing text in Firefox with "zoom text only" and hovering or focusing on the page tools, the text size increases but the highlighted area and the overall container doesn't. That makes it harder to understand which item is highlighted. And the bottom item overlaps with the bottom border and page content, making it harder to read.
That fails [[…] Resize [link]).

[image]


## Other non-fail accessibility issues

These don't strictly fail WCAG but are still accessibility issues. Fixing them is recommended but optional for passing WCAG.

* [ ] When resizing text in Firefox with "zoom text only", the page tool icons don't get bigger. That makes them harder to see for low vision users, especially combined with their low colour contrast (as listed in #3443).

* [ ] When using a screen magnifier, the page tools are much harder to notice and find on the page. As soon as you know where they are, that will be less of a problem, though.

* [ ] When I tested activating items in the page tools via voice control (Dragon), I was able to click on each item (via saying e.g. "click backlinks") but only because I knew what to say. You cannot hover over anything with voice control. You could tab to it, but voice control users rarely do that. Instead they would just click. And for that they would need to know what the thing is called that they want to click on. But if they've never seen the page tools open, they will never see their names. That means there is more cognitive load and uncertainty for people with motor impairments. They would probably rely on 'mouse grid' instead (which lets you zone in on things to click on) which takes longer to use than just saying what to click on.

title: Accessibility issues with footnotes
body:
* [ ] The footnote tooltips should have a way of closing them without using the mouse, like pressing ESC. Otherwise people who use keyboard only and don't use a mouse, like motor impaired people, will not be able close the tooltip and therefore read the text underneath it.
That fails [[…] Content on Hover or [link]).
[image]


## Other non-fail accessibility issues

These don't strictly fail WCAG but are still accessibility issues. Fixing them is recommended but optional for passing WCAG.

* [ ] It would be better if the list of footnotes at the bottom of the page had their own heading. That would make it easier for screen reader users to navigate to them and know about their position early on. And it would be better for usability as it makes it easier to understand what that section is.
[image]

* [ ] Footnote links could improve their link text to make it clearer that they are linking to a footnote. That gets more important for the links at the bottom when they link back. Otherwise the links won't make sense out of context when there are, for example, two links with the link text of "1" but which go to two very different section on the page and have a different functionality.
That could be fixed by adding more information to the `title`, like "go to footnote" and "go back to where this footnote was referenced" (ideally with not that many words).

* [ ] When code blocks are read out by screen readers, the semantics of them are not read out. That means it's not clear that they are code blocks at all. Although this uses the correct semantics, annoyingly screen readers don't honour them. (Maybe there is a setting that could do that, I don't know.)
One way to fix this is by adding some explanatory text and/or heading before the code block. That could even be visually hidden.

* [ ] The file name for the example code under ["Downloadable Code Blocks" on the syntax page](https://grimm.haz.wiki/wiki:syntax#downloadable_code_blocks) is "myexample.php". Nearly all screen readers read that as one word, so it's difficult to understand. It would be better as "MyExample.php" (camel case) or "my-example.php" (with dashes). Most screen readers read that word for word. This is only a minor issue, though.

title: Accessibility issues on the search results page
body:
Apart from #3459, there is only one more fail on the [search results page](https://grimm.haz.wiki/start?do=search&id=start&q=king) and a couple more non-fail issues.

* [ ] The main search field doesn't have an accessible name. It needs to have a `label`, ideally visible (but it can also be visually hidden or have an `aria-label` etc).
That fails [[…] Name, Role, [link]) and has a medium priority.

[image]


## Other non-fail accessibility issues

These don't strictly fail WCAG but are still accessibility issues. Fixing them is recommended but optional for passing WCAG.
These are all minor except for the magnification issue.

* [ ] The `fieldset` around the search field and filters doesn't have a `legend`.

* [ ] It's confusing and less discoverable seeing the search form when magnifying the screen because everything is centred. (Similar to what I reported about the login form in #3457.) The fieldset border and the input border look too similar, and when you cannot see the end of either, it's difficult to understand what it is. That's made worse because the input is missing a label and the fieldset is missing a legend, which makes them look less like form elements.
I would add the label and legend and left-align the form.
[image]

* [ ] The search terms are highlighted via the `strong` element. That is okay, but using the `mark` element would be more semantic (new since HTML5). Screen readers never announce `strong` but some announce `mark`.

* [ ] The search terms are not highlighted when in High Contrast Mode or when changing colours in Firefox. Using `mark` instead of `strong` (see above) would fix that. But this could also be fixed through other means, for example by giving the highlighting an invisible border or outline.
[image]
[image]

* [ ] The 'toggle search tools' button comes visually after the search field and button but comes before them in source and tab order. That's a bit confusing and unexpected.

* [ ] There are two 'search' buttons on the page, one in the header (the magnifier icon) and the other in the main content's search. Although they perform the same function, they are on two different forms and are not interchangeable. It would be better (for voice control and screen reader users) to give them unique names. Although I'm not sure with which words to differentiate them and if that might cause more confusion.

* [ ] The search results are using a description list (`dl` with `dt` and `dd`). Although that is semantically fine, unfortunately screen readers don't handle them very well and they are read out quite inconsistently. For example, NVDA just reads lines, and VoiceOver repeats "term" and especially "description" a lot. That's more something to be aware of and not necessarily to change.

* [ ] It is unclear what the purpose of the `@stories` links are and they make even less sense out of context. But they are equally unclear to everyone, which makes this a usability rather than an accessibility issue.

title: Icons and images
body:
Device: 

- Nokia 7.1, Android 10, TalkBack 13.  
- Pixel 4a, Android 12, TalkBack 13. 

The icons displayed in the instructions (onboarding), have no text alternative. People who use assistive devices will miss this information. 

Another example is after entering an URL (or hostname) and it's trying to connect with the server, there's an spinner icon in the screen. Users who are visually impaired have no idea that the server is connecting. 
Make sure that all icons, images and logo's displayed on the app have a text alternative (unless it's decorative).

title: [FEATURE] Need a mechanism for users to add alternative text for images uploaded.
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
(Accessibility issue with image uploading, no images have alternative text)
All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
[[…] [link])


**Describe the solution you'd like**
Currently, the uploader being used does not have a required field for "Alternative text" there for images are not being pronounced properly to users of assistive technology. It is inaccessible. Please add a field that is required, for "Alternative text" that explains to users (possibly with help text) that this is to describe the image for those that cannot see it. 

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Add a field or create a custom uploader. 

**Additional context**
This is anywhere in the app where user may upload a photo, or even in the events manager in the file upload field, there needs to be a field for alt text too.

title: Decide on using title vs aria-label
body: When we have buttons that only contain an icon and maybe in some other cases, we need to provide an alternative text ([WCAG [link])). There are a lot of options for that, but currently we use of of these two: - `aria-label`: `` - Common user agents ignore this attribute - In the [WAI ARIA Text Alternative Computation [link]) this attribute has a very high priority. - `title`: `` - Many user agents show the label as a tooltip on (long) hover. - The [HTML5 [link]) warns that "many user agents do not expose the [title] attribute in an accessible manner". - In the [WAI ARIA Text Alternative Computation [link]) the title attribute is used, but has a very low priority. Both options have pros and cons, but we should have clear rules on when to use which one.

# GUIDELINE ## Principle > PERCEIVABLE: Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. title: [Portals] DOM order accessibility
body:
**Components built with Portals include accessibility defects leading to poor usability/task abandonment.**

During accessibility audits and usability testing of Shopify components, we’ve noticed a prominent defect with components built with Portals; DOM structure.

Portals sets dynamically generated content containers at the bottom of the DOM. This is fine for modal window components since keyboard focus is explicitly placed on/within the modal container. The Portals documentation even calls this out and links to APG for more documentation.

The issue lies with other component patterns; [link]) (popovers, drop-down navigation, etc,) [link]), [link]), etc. The expectation for these components is for focus to **remain** on the activator and for dynamic content containers to appear **next** in the DOM, a direct sibling to the related activator control.

For example, during usability testing, testers struggled to use one such component which was built using Portals. When the dynamic container appeared after interacting with the activator, testers would move their screen reader virtual cursor forward from the activator, expecting to interact with the dynamic content. Instead, the cursor moved "underneath" the container, bypassing the content, to the next (unrelated) item in the DOM. This led to a confusing user experience.

In addition, this issue is a violation of WCAG [[…]: Meaningful [link]) (Level A.) Specifically, [Failure of […] due to changing the meaning of content by positioning information with [link]).

**Is it possible to adjust the position of the dynamic content container to be a sibling of the activator?**

This would be a big win for accessibility, not only for Shopify components built with Portals, but for all platforms.

title: A11y: structure of article overviews could be improved
body:
https://next.smashingmagazine.com/articles/

Inspect article previews.

One issue is tab order (and perhaps reading order in screen reader) doesn't follow document order and document semantics. This could be a […] failure, although not super bad here as the previews are short.

Normally you read and tab through the header, main content, then footer, and your eyes move from left to right, top to bottom (for roman languages). With this layout, the footer is in the right hand column, but placed before the main content in the DOM (and thus tab order)

See screenshot of screen reader reading order and tab order (red and blue respectively...sorry about the finger drawing, I left my pen at work)
[image]

This is easy to fix by moving the footer element below the content (last element in the article element).  
this works without any style fixes and makes the document structure correct too (footer at the foot of the article).

The next issue may be a bit more tricky as it requires CSS changes.

Currently there is a header element inside the article (so far so good), but the h2 heading is outside the heading. This makes an odd document outline. It should be inside (note browsers don't need to report headers and footers inside articles to the a11y layer per html aam spec usually just relying on the h* element, but your mileage may vary with different browser/sr combinations.

The next thing that is off is that inside the heading is a figure element (without any figcaption so it has no accessible name; see https://w3c.github.io/html-aam/#h-figure-element-accessible-name-computation). 

In this case I don't think the author portrait is a figure of the article. It is really decoration, as the author name is visibly along side it (leading to the name read twice, which was reported as another issue). Instead it would be better to remove the figure and just have `img alt=""`. You probably want it as a link, but you can just include it in the same anchor where the author name is included.

The whole img, author name and "wrote" span could be a paragraph above the h2 inside the header element, or arguably as it is meant to be all read together as one sentence, they could be a span inside the h2 (depends if you want that as one span of text as the accessible name of the article heading and if you want it read when the user navigates by headings on the page or not.

body:
[…]:

> Instructions do not rely upon shape, size, or visual location (e.g., "Click the square icon
to continue" or "Instructions are in the right-hand column".)

title: Do not block orientation if not essencial
body:
This is a "not-end" requirement. What I want to mean is that this should be considered for any new page you create that Student can access. Also should correct the old pages.

I will use the label **Feature Design Notes** to this cases
 
***************
[…]
 **Content does not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, such as portrait or landscape, unless a specific display orientation is essential.**

**NOTE**
Many users will expect to use OS-level settings to prevent the orientation from changing. As a result, it is usually preferable to satisfy this Success Criterion by not restricting the content's ability to adapt to changes in orientation and allowing users to use the OS orientation lock when desired.

**NOTE 2**
Exception: Orientation locking is allowed if a specific orientation is essential to the underlying functionality (such as a banking application that requires horizontal orientation when photographing a check for deposit).
ESSENTIAL: if removed, would fundamentally change the information or functionality of the content, and information and functionality cannot be achieved in another way that would conform

# Users
- Users with dexterity impairments, who have a mounted device will be able to use the content in their fixed orientation.
- Users with low-vision will be able to view content in the orientation that works best for them, for example to increase the text size by viewing content in landscape.
- A person who cannot hold the device and has it mounted attached to a wheelchair or bed.
***********************
- [ ] Do not lock the content orientation unless a specific orientation is essential to the functionality.

# Examples

- Example 1: Online video site
A video is shown in either portrait or in landscape based on the user's chosen orientation.
- Example 2: Messaging website
A messaging website can display messages in both portrait and landscape orientations.
- Example 3: eReader web app
An eReader web app can display the contents of a book in both portrait and landscape orientation.
- Example 4: Check deposit in banking app
An example where orientation is essential could be a banking app that requires the device be in landscape mode to easily and accurately capture an image of a check for deposit. These paper forms are typically about twice as wide as they are high.
- Example 5: Piano app
An example where orientation is essential could be a piano app that requires the device to be in landscape mode to allow room for enough of the piano keys to be functionally usable. Since a piano app is emulating a physical piano keyboard that needs to retain relative physical characteristics between keys, either too few keys would be available, or the keys would be much too narrow.

# Test Procedure

1. Open the content in landscape view. Check that the content is oriented for this view.
2. Open the content in portrait view. Check that the content is oriented for this view.
3. If there are any controls in the content, user agent, operating system, or device that restrict or allow orientation changes, check that the controls can be set to allow checks one and two to be true.
    1. Check for a control within the user interface to change the orientation of the content.
     1. Check that when the control is operated that the content changes orientation.

Expected Results: Checks 1 and 2 are true; If 3 is true, checks i and ii must be true.
If a specific orientation is determined to be essential for the operation and viewing of the content, then this failure not apply.
